outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: Facts, Parties, and the Path to Federal Court
outline.description: This chapter introduces the petitioners, the events in Colombia that formed the basis of their claims, and the immigration proceedings that led to the Tenth Circuit’s review. It helps students distinguish between the political activity, the property dispute, the threats, and the family’s departure from Colombia, because those factual strands are central to the court’s later analysis.
subtopics: The petitioners: a Colombian family from Bogota involved in a furniture business
Their political activity: membership in the Colombian Liberal Party and support for Federico Gutierrez in the 2022 presidential election
Initial politically tinged threats received during campaign activity
Jimenez’s legal and prosecutorial background: law student, provisional lawyer, and intern in the National Prosecutor’s office
The San Bernardo property dispute and Jimenez’s involvement on behalf of a client
Discovery that the tenant was Rafael Augusto Montanez Lancheros ('Don Rafa') and the property’s connection to trafficking, prostitution, kidnapping, and murder
Escalation of events: threatening brochure, gunpoint confrontation at the factory, threats to employees, and the school incident involving the younger son
Temporary move to Jimenez’s mother’s home and the family’s decision to leave Colombia
Contacts with police officers before departure and the officers’ alleged responses
Removal proceedings in the United States: Notices to Appear, conceded removability, and applications for asylum, withholding, and CAT protection
The IJ’s ruling, the BIA’s affirmance, and the narrowed issues presented to the Tenth Circuit

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Standard of Review and the Asylum/Withholding Framework
outline.description: This chapter explains the procedural lens through which the Tenth Circuit reviewed the case and sets out the legal requirements for asylum and withholding of removal. It clarifies why the court repeatedly asks whether substantial evidence supports the BIA, rather than deciding the facts anew.
subtopics: Jurisdiction under 8 U.S.C. § 1252 to review final orders of removal
The court’s focus on the BIA decision, with permissible consultation of the IJ’s fuller reasoning
Substantial-evidence review: when factual findings are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to disagree
Asylum as discretionary relief and the applicant’s burden to prove refugee status by a preponderance of the evidence
Statutory definition of 'refugee' and the protected grounds
Past persecution as one route to refugee status and the rebuttable presumption of future persecution
The three core elements of a past-persecution claim: qualifying harm, nexus to a protected ground, and government involvement or inability/unwillingness to control private actors
The relationship between asylum and withholding of removal, including why failure on asylum generally defeats withholding when the same theory is advanced
Issues abandoned on appeal: CAT protection and due process/right-to-counsel arguments

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: Why the Court Found No Past Persecution
outline.description: This chapter examines the court’s treatment of the harm element. It shows how the Tenth Circuit applied its case law on threats, emotional distress, and cumulative harm, and why it concluded that the family’s experiences, though serious and frightening, did not compel a finding of past persecution.
subtopics: The INA’s lack of a statutory definition of persecution and the Tenth Circuit’s judicial standard
Persecution as suffering or harm that is more than mere restrictions or threats
The cumulative-harm approach: assessing all incidents together rather than in isolation
The role of threats in persecution analysis and the court’s statement that threats alone are generally insufficient
Petitioners’ concession that they suffered no lasting physical harm and the significance of that concession
Emotional and psychological harm asserted by the family, including Duarte’s sleep problems and the child’s panic attacks
Why the court viewed psychological distress stemming from threats as insufficient on this record
Use of Tenth Circuit precedent comparing more severe facts that still did not qualify as persecution
How the substantial-evidence standard shaped the outcome: the court did not ask whether persecution could be found, but whether the record compelled it
The holding on this element: substantial evidence supported the BIA’s conclusion that the aggregate harm did not rise to past persecution

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: Nexus to Political Opinion and the Court’s Mixed-Motive Analysis
outline.description: This chapter focuses on causation. It explains why the petitioners’ political-opinion theory failed even though political references appeared in some threats, and how the court concluded that Don Rafa’s main motive was protecting his criminal operation and property interests rather than punishing opposition politics.
subtopics: The petitioners’ narrowed nexus argument on appeal: political opinion rather than particular social group
The statutory requirement that a protected ground be 'at least one central reason' for the persecution
What it means for a reason to be central rather than incidental, tangential, superficial, subordinate, or minor
Mixed-motive persecution and the need for a protected ground to remain central even when other motives exist
Evidence supporting the political-opinion theory: Liberal Party activity, support for a rival candidate, and references to 'Liberal Party' in threats
Evidence undermining that theory: escalation after Jimenez’s involvement with Don Rafa’s property and investigation
The significance of accusations that Jimenez was a 'snitch' for the prosecutor’s office and responsible for searches and seizures
The court’s distinction between early campaign-related threats and later targeted threats linked to Don Rafa
Why the court concluded the predominant motive was Jimenez’s professional and personal interference with Don Rafa’s interests
The deferential review principle against reweighing evidence and its effect on the nexus holding

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 5: Government Protection, Internal Relocation, and Final Disposition
outline.description: This chapter addresses the remaining elements necessary for asylum based on private-actor harm: whether the Colombian government was unable or unwilling to protect the family and whether relocation within Colombia was reasonably possible. It concludes with the court’s disposition and the implications for withholding of removal.
subtopics: Why government inability or unwillingness matters when the alleged persecutors are private actors
The role of notice to the government and the importance of reporting persecution
When failure to report is not fatal: futility or danger as possible excuses
The petitioners’ limited efforts to seek protection and the court’s characterization of those efforts as minimal
The evidentiary weakness of relying on conversations with two police officers as proof of nationwide governmental inability or unwillingness
The court’s emphasis that neither Jimenez nor his father used their government or law-enforcement connections to make a fuller report
Why the record cut against the claim of futility: authorities had already attempted searches and seizures at Don Rafa’s property
The court’s conclusion that petitioners failed to show the Colombian government would not or could not protect them
Internal relocation doctrine and its place in rebutting fear of future persecution
Facts supporting safe relocation: family remaining in Colombia unharmed, father still working in the criminal justice system, and the family’s uneventful three-week stay in the Bogota countryside
The court’s reliance on the persecutors’ command to leave the neighborhood rather than the country
Disposition: denial of asylum, automatic failure of the higher-standard withholding claim, and denial of the petition for review
